title: The complexity of scientific optimism: A review of "It Could Be Otherwise"
gist: A review of neurobiologist Stuart Firestein's book It Could Be Otherwise (Basic Books, 2026), which argues that optimism—not just conflict—has always driven scientific progress, and pushes back against determinism as a force that shrinks scientific imagination by oversimplifying complex natural systems.

themes.theme: Optimism as an engine of science

insights.claim: Neurobiologist Stuart Firestein argues in It Could Be Otherwise (Basic Books, 2026) that optimism, as much as conflict, has always been a character in the development of modern science and should be explicitly named and clarified.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Reframes the cultural narrative of science from adversarial struggle to optimism-driven progress—relevant to how research institutions and funders motivate long-horizon work.
insights.quote: optimism, as much as conflict, has always been a character in the development of modern science, and that it should be named and clarified
insights.locator: In It Could Be Otherwise (Basic Books, 2026), neurobiologist and SFI Fractal Faculty

insights.claim: Firestein contends that naming optimism as a driver of science is consistent with the history of scientific progress and can lead to a more creative and integrative scientific endeavor better equipped to study the natural world.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Suggests methodological upside—embracing optimism could broaden which problems scientists are willing to tackle.
insights.locator: Doing so, he argues, is not only consistent with the history

insights.claim: The reviewer frames science's tolerance for failure—failed experiments, broken theories, and journal rejections—as evidence that the discipline fundamentally runs on optimism, the belief that a better truth is possible.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: A lens for evaluating research culture: persistence through failure is a signal of underlying optimism, not merely grit.
insights.quote: To do science well and rigorously, we must believe that a better truth is possible.
insights.locator: This is the reason we tolerate failed experiments

themes.theme: Preconditions for the idea of progress

insights.claim: Firestein argues that the notion of scientific progress requires three ingredients: a linear view of time, a belief that the universe is law-abiding, and broad public accessibility of ideas so their triumphs are appreciated.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: A checklist for what cultural conditions must hold for a society to sustain a belief in scientific progress.
insights.quote: it requires a linear view of time, a belief in the notion that the universe is law-abiding, and a broad accessibility of ideas
insights.locator: Firestein explains how the notion of progress has been built

insights.claim: The book claims science has already carried a hidden positivist agenda—a historical arrow running from ignorance to knowledge production—with optimism operating in its margins.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Names an implicit ideology in science that shapes what counts as progress—useful for critiquing linear-progress assumptions.
insights.quote: there is a historical arrow from ignorance to knowledge production, and optimism operates in these margins
insights.locator: how science has already carried a hidden positivist agenda

insights.claim: Firestein's target is not pessimism but determinism—the notion that the apparent caprice of natural systems can be neatly resolved into laws and axioms—which he argues shrinks the scientific imagination.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Positions over-formalization as a liability, not a virtue—a caution against models that assume natural systems are fully reducible.
insights.quote: Not against pessimism, but against its close relative, determinism: the notion that the apparent caprice of natural systems can be neatly resolved into laws and axioms.
insights.locator: What then, is Firestein pushing back against?

insights.claim: In Chapter 4, titled "F—— the Enlightenment," Firestein critiques the Enlightenment's attempt to compress complex natural phenomena into neat formalisms.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Signals the book's provocative stance against reductionist formalism—a talking point for complexity-science positioning.
insights.quote: If everything is all worked out, inexorably proceeding like the ticks of a clock ever since the Big Bang…then what’s the point, really?

insights.claim: The book skillfully distinguishes terms that are often confounded—complexity, irreducible complexity, and uncertainty—and makes the caveat that determinism can co-exist with unpredictability.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: A conceptual disambiguation useful to anyone modeling systems where deterministic rules still yield unpredictable outcomes.
insights.quote: the especially important caveat that determinism can co-exist with unpredictability

insights.claim: Firestein situates Darwin's legacy as a triumph of contingency in natural systems, arguing Darwinism's grander message was to study natural systems with an appreciation for idiosyncrasy as a main feature.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Elevates contingency and idiosyncrasy over mechanism as the enduring lesson of evolutionary science.
insights.quote: The triumph of Darwinism is not only about the specific mechanism for evolution, but about the grander message it communicated for how to study natural systems

insights.claim: Firestein argues the triumphs of complexity science—chaos and emergence—are subversive because they are fully consistent with rigorous scientific research and provide rigorous formalisms, yet embrace the capriciousness of natural systems.
insights.speaker: Santa Fe Institute
insights.so_what: Frames complexity science as the reconciliation of rigor and unpredictability—central to the Santa Fe Institute's intellectual brand.
insights.quote: they are perfectly consistent with our manner of conducting scientific research and provide rigorous formalisms, yet embrace the capriciousness of natural systems
insights.locator: what makes the triumphs of complexity science
